description:
Found s393 while diagnosing #315.  op/select.t line 11 is

    plan reverse 9;

and PCL's TAP layer dies with `plan(): unrecognized plan form (#(N))`, so the
file produces NO TAP — C_ok 0, and the sweep can say nothing about it.

RULED OUT BY PROBE (do not re-derive): argument flattening is NOT the bug.
`f(reverse 9)` and the paren-less `f reverse 9` both hand ONE flattened arg to
a perl sub, matching perl exactly.  The difference is that `plan` is a RUNTIME
function in cl/pcl-test.lisp, so it receives the value of `(p-reverse 9)`
directly — a one-element VECTOR — and its form dispatch (which knows
`tests => N`, `skip_all => …`, and a bare count) has no case for it.

DYING IS CORRECT — #202 made `plan` the ONE assertion that may die, precisely
so an unjudgeable plan is loud.  The fix is to recognise the legal perl
spelling first: a plan argument that arrives as a 1-element aggregate is the
count, exactly as perl's list-context `plan(reverse 9)` is.  Keep the die for
what remains unrecognised, and keep it naming the form.

BAR: the guard row goes in Pl/t (a run row through the TAP layer), then
re-measure op/select.t and splice its snapshot row.  cl/pcl-test.lisp is in
the sweep's reach, so the full sweep is NOT optional for this one.</description>


=== DONE s395d.  Fixed at the layer the probe pointed to, not the one the task guessed: `plan` is a perl SUB in t/test.pl, so its argument list FLATTENS; pl-plan is a CL function and got the unflattened vector.  It now spreads through p-flatten-args -- the same spreading a p-sub does to build @_ -- so there is no second flattening rule and no `1-element aggregate` special case.  op/select.t 0 -> 3 ok / 6 not-ok (the 6 are `select` returning the glob/ref, a different gap).  Guard: 1 row in Pl/t/tap-assert-01.t.
subject: TAP plan(): `plan reverse 9;` dies "unrecognized plan form (#(N))" — op/select.t produces no TAP at all
